How Gene Survival Can Produce Cooperation An animal risks danger to protect its young. Another competes fiercely with its relatives. How can natural selection produce both care and conflict?
Richard Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene, first published in 1976, approaches these questions through inherited information. Bodies live and die. Copies of genes can persist through many generations. Dawkins asks readers to explain adaptations by considering which inherited variants leave more copies. The Oxford University Press description identifies this gene-centered view as the book’s central argument.
The title creates a common misunderstanding. Genes have no intentions or moral character. “Selfish” describes a pattern of propagation. A variant can spread through behavior that helps another animal. In an interview with PBS, Dawkins explicitly distinguishes gene selfishness from individual selfishness. Much of the book explains how cooperation becomes possible within this framework.
Genes Persist Through Changing Bodies A replicator is something whose structure can be copied. In biological evolution, genetic sequences carry inherited information. Copying introduces variation, and some variants contribute to their own transmission more effectively than others. Repeated across generations, differences in transmission can change a population.
An organism provides the working system through which many genetic effects occur. Its genes function together, within cells and environments. Calling genes replicators does not mean that DNA copies itself without cellular machinery. Nor does it mean that one gene independently builds a whole behavior.
The distinction becomes especially useful when genetic interests diverge. A genetic element can sometimes spread at a cost to the organism carrying it. Conversely, many genes spread because their effects help the whole organism survive and reproduce. The research review on selfish genetic elements examines this relationship between genetic cooperation and conflict.
The useful question is therefore specific: compared with an alternative inherited variant, under what conditions would this variant become more common? Describing something as beneficial to life in general does not answer that question.
Helping Relatives Can Preserve Copies of Genes An animal’s own offspring are one route by which inherited variants continue. Relatives provide another route because they may carry copies inherited from common ancestors.
This is the basis of kin selection. A costly helping behavior can spread when its reproductive benefit to relatives, weighted by relatedness, exceeds its reproductive cost to the helper. The familiar shorthand is rB > C. Relatedness is represented by r, benefit by B, and cost by C. These costs concern reproductive consequences, rather than effort alone.
For an illustrative case, consider a bird that helps raise close relatives instead of attempting to breed alone. Helping could be favored if it produces enough additional surviving relatives, after accounting for its lost breeding opportunities. Relatedness alone cannot settle the result. Food, nest access, and the actual effect of help also matter.
Dawkins makes accessible the logic developed in W. D. Hamilton’s work on inclusive fitness. An animal need not recognize DNA or calculate an equation. Selection can favor behavioral responses to cues that reliably track these conditions.
Families Combine Shared Interests and Conflict Kinship creates overlapping interests. It does not make every family member’s evolutionary interests identical.
A parent must divide limited resources among present and possible future offspring. An offspring receives the whole direct benefit of extra food for itself. It receives only an indirect genetic benefit when that food supports a sibling. The amount of care favored from one perspective can therefore differ from the amount favored from the other.
Weaning makes the disagreement concrete. Continued feeding can benefit a young mammal while reducing the mother’s ability to support other offspring. There can be a period when further feeding favors the young animal’s genetic interests but no longer favors the mother’s allocation across offspring. This reasoning comes from Robert Trivers’s theory of parent–offspring conflict.
The explanation does not require a young animal to plan exploitation. Selection can shape begging, resistance, and parental responses without conscious calculation. Care and conflict can coexist because family members share some interests and differ over others. This is an account of possible evolutionary pressures, rather than a diagnosis of every disagreement in a human family.
Reproduction Involves Trade-offs Between Partners Parents can also differ over how much care each should provide. Both may benefit from surviving offspring. Each may also gain from leaving more of the work to the other, if that frees resources for further reproduction.
Parental investment includes resources devoted to an offspring that reduce the parent’s ability to invest elsewhere. Producing eggs, guarding a nest, and feeding young can all contribute. The relevant quantity is the opportunity lost, rather than the visible size of the task.
Drawing on Trivers’s account of parental investment and sexual selection, Dawkins connects unequal investment with competition for mates and mate choice. These are conditional arguments. Which parent cares, and which sex competes more intensely, depends on the species and its breeding conditions. The framework calls for ecological evidence before making claims about a particular population.
The Best Strategy Depends on Other Animals Natural selection does not always favor maximum aggression. Fighting can secure a resource, but injury can erase that advantage.
Dawkins uses evolutionary game theory to explain such trade-offs. In the hawk–dove model, “hawk” and “dove” name strategies rather than actual bird species. Hawks escalate contests. Doves avoid serious fighting. An aggressive strategy can prosper among opponents that retreat. When escalation becomes common, the costs of fighting can make restraint more successful.
An evolutionarily stable strategy can resist invasion by a rare alternative under the model’s conditions. Stability concerns relative success in a population. It does not imply kindness, perfect design, or the best outcome for everyone.
The foundational paper by John Maynard Smith and George Price showed how limited conflict could arise through advantages to individuals without assuming that animals restrain themselves to protect their species.
The broader lesson is to examine the surrounding population. A behavior that succeeds when rare may fail when common. Its value depends on what others do and on the costs of their encounters.
Repeated Encounters Can Support Cooperation Helping need not depend on close kinship. Repeated encounters can make present cooperation worthwhile because it affects future treatment.
Later editions develop this through the repeated prisoner’s dilemma. Two participants can both gain from cooperation, while each faces an immediate temptation to exploit the other. If encounters continue, exploitation can trigger responses that reduce its long-term return.
Dawkins discusses Robert Axelrod’s computer tournaments and the simple Tit for Tat strategy. It cooperates first, then repeats the partner’s previous action. It can sustain mutual cooperation while responding to defection. Axelrod and Hamilton’s original paper analyzes conditions under which reciprocal cooperation can arise and resist invasion.
This is a model result, rather than a universal instruction for relationships. Outcomes depend on future encounters, available strategies, and the costs and benefits of each action. As a practical interpretation, cooperation deserves attention to its supporting conditions: reliable repeated contact and responses that discourage exploitation. A model cannot establish that one response will work in every social setting.
Memes Extend the Question Beyond DNA Dawkins introduces memes as culturally transmitted units, such as tunes or ideas. They spread through learning and imitation. Their success in transmission need not match their truth or their benefit to people.
This is an extension of the replicator argument. It invites readers to ask what makes cultural material easy to retain and pass on. It remains an analogy: people interpret and modify ideas, and cultural units are harder to define than DNA sequences. Popularity alone does not demonstrate a complete evolutionary explanation.
Genetic Effects Can Reach Outside a Body Later editions also introduce the extended phenotype. A gene’s effects need not stop at an organism’s skin. A caddis larva’s protective case illustrates how inherited influences on building behavior can affect an external structure. Selection can act through the structure’s consequences for survival and reproduction. These extensions appear in the book’s later-edition text.
What This Perspective Explains—and Its Limits The book offers a powerful method for testing explanations of adaptation. Identify inherited variation, trace its effects, and ask how those effects change transmission. A plausible story still needs evidence about mechanisms and reproductive consequences.
The gene-centered perspective also belongs within a wider debate about levels of selection. Later multilevel-selection modeling shows how cooperation can be favored through differences between groups even when competition within groups favors noncooperators. This does not make every appeal to group benefit valid. It requires an explicit account of group formation, reproduction, and competition.
Finally, an evolutionary explanation does not establish an ethical rule. Dawkins rejects that inference in his PBS interview. Genetic influences are also not a claim that experience and learning cannot change behavior.
My main takeaway is a habit of explanation: distinguish the interests of genes, individuals, relatives, and groups. Then identify the conditions that connect them. That habit makes both cooperation and conflict easier to investigate, while leaving moral choices to moral reasoning.
Sources Oxford University Press: book identity, overview, and later-edition contents; Dawkins’s book text, hosted by Loyola Marymount University. PBS: Dawkins on altruism, genetic influence, and morality. Hamilton: inclusive fitness; Trivers: parent–offspring conflict and parental investment. Maynard Smith and Price: animal conflict; Axelrod and Hamilton: reciprocal cooperation. Later context: selfish genetic elements and the gene-centered view; Traulsen and Nowak: multilevel selection.

Life’s History Includes Both Branches and Connections A family tree traces inheritance from parents to offspring. Extend that pattern across species, and evolution appears as a great branching tree. Each lineage divides. Its descendants carry the history of that branch.
David Quammen’s The Tangled Tree: A Radical New History of Life explains why this picture is incomplete. Genes can also move between separate lineages. Cells can become lasting parts of other cells. An organism can therefore contain genetic material with several different histories.
Quammen follows the scientists who uncovered these connections. His central argument is that molecular evidence changes both the shape of life’s history and our place within it. Humans belong to branching lineages, but our cells also preserve ancient biological mergers. The publisher’s description identifies horizontal gene transfer as a central thread.
Reading Ancestry in Molecules Visible features help scientists compare animals and plants. They provide fewer clues for many microbes. Two cells can look similar under a microscope while having deeply different evolutionary histories.
Molecular comparisons offered another route. DNA and RNA contain sequences of chemical units. Inherited changes in those sequences can help researchers infer relationships. Molecular phylogenetics uses such evidence to reconstruct evolutionary ancestry.
Carl Woese made ribosomal RNA central to this work. Ribosomes build proteins, and all cellular life depends on them. Their RNA offered a basis for comparing organisms across enormous evolutionary distances.
Woese and his colleagues had to assemble these comparisons through painstaking laboratory work. The important change was conceptual as well as technical: organisms could be grouped by molecular evidence rather than appearance alone. Quammen presents Woese’s research as a major turning point in the investigation of deep ancestry.
Archaea Redraw the Map Woese and George Fox found that methane-producing microbes did not fit among ordinary bacteria. Their ribosomal RNA indicated a separate, deeply divergent lineage. Their 1977 paper helped establish the organisms now called archaea.
This discovery challenged the simple division between cells with a nucleus and cells without one. Bacteria and archaea both lack a membrane-bound nucleus. That shared feature does not make them one close evolutionary group.
Woese’s work eventually supported a three-domain framework: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. Eukarya includes animals, plants, fungi, and other organisms whose cells have nuclei. Humans occupy one small part of that larger map.
The discovery also illustrates a recurring problem in classification. A category can collect organisms that share a visible feature without capturing their deepest relationships. A new measuring method can reveal differences that the old method could not detect.
Genes Can Move Sideways Vertical inheritance passes genetic material from a parent to its offspring. Horizontal gene transfer moves genetic material between organisms outside that parent–offspring route. It can cross species boundaries.
This is more than hybridization between close relatives. A microbe can acquire a useful gene from another lineage without the two organisms producing a hybrid offspring.
Bacteria have several routes for such exchange. They can take up DNA released into their surroundings. Viruses that infect bacteria can carry DNA between cells. Cells can also transfer DNA through direct contact, often using plasmids: small DNA molecules separate from the main chromosome. These mechanisms are described in the NCBI-hosted chapter on bacterial genetics.
Transfer does not guarantee lasting evolutionary change. The incoming material must survive and persist. If it becomes established, however, descendants can inherit it vertically. A sideways acquisition can become part of a lineage’s continuing family history.
Why One Gene Cannot Tell Every Story Imagine two microbial lineages that separated long ago. Later, one receives a gene from the other. Most of its genome still reflects its earlier ancestry. The transferred gene records a more recent connection.
This illustrative case explains why different genes can produce different evolutionary trees. Researchers may be tracking different histories within the same organism. A disagreement among trees is not automatically a laboratory mistake.
Ford Doolittle is an important figure in Quammen’s account of this problem. His 1999 analysis argues that genomes assembled from multiple sources challenge the idea of one universal hierarchy that captures every relationship.
The implication is precise. A tree can represent the history of a particular gene or many inherited cellular features. It may fail to represent every part of a genome at once. For questions involving extensive transfer, a network can show connections that a strictly branching picture leaves out.
Margulis and the Merger Within the Cell Lynn Margulis developed another challenge to a history made only of splitting branches. Endosymbiosis occurs when one organism lives within another. Her evolutionary argument was that some internal cell structures began as separate organisms and became permanent partners.
Mitochondria, which help cells obtain usable energy, descend from bacteria. Chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae, also have bacterial origins. Their incorporation made earlier partnerships part of the structure of later cells.
Margulis’s 1967 paper, published under the name Lynn Sagan, set out a testable account of cell origins. Her wider proposal also included a symbiotic origin for structures associated with flagella. That part did not gain the same support as the bacterial origins of mitochondria and chloroplasts.
Endosymbiosis and gene transfer are connected but distinct processes. One incorporates a cellular partner. The other transfers genetic material. Both show how evolutionary lineages can contribute to a shared biological system.
Antibiotic Resistance Makes the Idea Concrete The consequences reach far beyond ancient history. Quammen discusses Tsutomu Watanabe’s work on transferable drug resistance. Bacteria could acquire resistance from other bacteria rather than develop every resistance trait independently.
Plasmids can carry several resistance genes together. A recipient may therefore gain a package of traits. Watanabe reviewed this phenomenon in “Infective Heredity of Multiple Drug Resistance in Bacteria”.
Mutation, transfer, and selection have different roles. Mutation can generate variation. Transfer can move existing genetic capabilities into another organism. Antibiotic exposure can then favor bacteria that carry resistance. Horizontal transfer expands the routes by which variation spreads; natural selection still affects which variants persist.
A practical implication is that tracking only a bacterial species can miss part of the problem. Resistance genes and the elements that carry them also have histories of movement. Evolutionary relationships can help explain an immediate public-health challenge.
Humans Carry Evidence of Ancient Encounters Quammen extends the argument to human identity. Our evolutionary history includes the bacterial ancestry of mitochondria and genetic material left by ancient viral infections. His account of the book emphasizes these mixed origins.
For a viral sequence to enter a continuing human lineage, it must reach genetic material that can pass to descendants. An ordinary infection does not automatically become hereditary. Once an insertion becomes established, later generations can receive it through ordinary reproduction.
Some inherited viral material has acquired useful functions. Research on syncytin identified a protein derived from a retroviral envelope gene that helps cells fuse during placental development. The original study supplies a concrete example of biological reuse.
This does not mean that humans are simply viruses or bacteria. It means that familiar structures and functions can have unexpected origins. Present biological roles do not always reveal the history of the components that perform them.
Reading the Scientific Revolution Carefully Quammen builds his history around researchers, including their disagreements and competing interpretations. That makes difficult ideas easier to follow. It also invites a useful distinction: a scientist can make a major discovery without being right about every wider claim.
The same care applies to the tree metaphor. Quammen explains in an author interview that branching remains important. His argument adds significant connections to that pattern. It does not discard common descent or natural selection.
The book appeared in 2018, and the deepest relationships remain active research questions. As a later update, a 2025 study of Asgard archaea places eukaryotes within that archaeal group. This supports a two-domain account of deep cellular ancestry rather than three equally separate founding branches. The exact placement of eukaryotes within archaea continues to be refined.
My main takeaway is to ask what history a biological claim describes. Is it the history of a species, a cell structure, or a particular gene? Those histories can overlap without being identical. Quammen’s achievement is to make those differences visible while showing how closely they connect all living things.
Sources Simon & Schuster: book identity, author credit, and overview; David Quammen: the author’s book page. Living on Earth: interview with Quammen about the book. Woese and Fox: original molecular classification research; Doolittle: the universal-tree problem. Margulis, writing as Sagan: original endosymbiosis paper; Watanabe: transferable drug resistance. Mi and colleagues: original syncytin study. Nature, 2025: later evidence on eukaryotic origins within Asgard archaea. This updates the context beyond the book.
